shots.phrase: Distributed systems operate across multiple networked computers where components inevitably experience partial failure.
When a node slows down, it becomes indistinguishable from a crashed server, forcing designers to make explicit assumptions about timing and communication.
This uncertainty means we cannot rely on simple timeouts to detect outages.
Instead, we must design protocols that tolerate delayed messages, duplicated transmissions, and unpredictable network schedules.

Understanding these constraints is the first step toward building reliable consensus mechanisms that survive real-world network chaos without assuming perfect synchronization or instantaneous failure detection.
To guarantee consistency across multiple nodes, we replicate state machines that process identical operations in the exact same order.
Each server maintains a local copy of the system state, but the critical challenge is ensuring they apply operations in identical sequences despite network delays.
If servers apply commands differently, the system diverges into conflicting states.
By forcing all nodes to execute the same sequence of operations, we eliminate state divergence.

This approach transforms distributed coordination into a single-threaded execution problem, where correctness depends entirely on the order of applied operations rather than complex distributed state synchronization.
To enforce identical execution order, we use a replicated log where every command is appended as a sequential entry.
Each log entry contains a unique term number and a sequence index, creating a total order across all servers.
When a client submits a request, the leader appends it to its log before acknowledging success.
Followers replicate the entry by appending it to their own logs at the same index.
This log structure ensures that every server records the exact same operations in the exact same order.
The log becomes the single source of truth for system state, preventing conflicting histories and enabling reliable recovery after crashes or network partitions.
A leader is elected to coordinate log replication and client requests.
Servers start as followers and transition to candidates when they miss heartbeats.
Randomized election timeouts prevent split votes by staggering candidate timeouts.
When a candidate requests votes, it increments a term number and includes its log's last entry.
Followers grant votes only if the candidate's log is at least as up-to-date.
Once a candidate receives votes from a majority, it becomes leader for that term.
Terms provide a logical clock that prevents stale leaders from interfering with newer elections, ensuring only the most recent leader can commit entries and maintain system progress.
Progress requires a majority quorum of nodes to agree on log entries and leadership.
A majority ensures that any two quorums share at least one node, preventing conflicting decisions.
If a network partition isolates a minority, the majority partition continues operating while the minority stalls.
This design prioritizes safety over availability during splits.
The quorum requirement guarantees that committed entries are durable across restarts and that only one leader can exist per term.
Without a majority, the system cannot safely commit operations or elect a new leader, ensuring that conflicting histories are never permitted during network failures.
The leader replicates log entries to followers by sending AppendEntries RPCs.
Each RPC includes the leader's term, the index of the entry to replicate, and the entry itself.
Followers respond with success or failure based on log matching.
If a follower's log conflicts, the leader backs off and retries with a lower index.
This process ensures all followers eventually match the leader's log.
The log-matching property guarantees that if two logs contain an entry with the same index and term, all preceding entries are identical.
This property enables reliable recovery and prevents divergent states during message loss or server restarts, maintaining a consistent replicated log across the cluster.
An entry becomes committed when it is replicated to a majority of servers and the leader's term matches the entry's term.
This rule ensures that only entries from the current leader are committed, preventing stale leaders from overwriting newer data.
Once committed, the entry is applied to the state machine in order.
The commit rule relies on the log-matching property to guarantee that all servers applying the entry share identical preceding history.
This prevents conflicting state updates and ensures that committed operations are durable across crashes.
The term-based commitment rule also handles leader changes gracefully, ensuring that only the most recent leader's entries are finalized.
Safety ensures that committed entries are never lost or overwritten, while liveness guarantees that the system continues making progress.
Raft prioritizes safety by refusing to commit entries from stale leaders and requiring majority agreement.
Liveness is maintained through randomized election timeouts and leader heartbeats.
When a leader fails, followers detect the absence of heartbeats and trigger elections.
If a majority is available, a new leader is elected and replication resumes.
If a minority is isolated, the system stalls but remains safe.
This trade-off ensures that the system never commits conflicting histories, even at the cost of temporary unavailability during network partitions or leader failures.
Clients must retry operations when they receive no response, but retries can cause duplicate commands if the original request succeeded.
To handle this, clients include a unique request ID with each operation.
The server checks if the ID has already been processed and returns the cached result if so.
This idempotency mechanism prevents duplicate state updates.
Retries are essential for availability during network delays or leader elections.
By combining unique request IDs with server-side deduplication, clients can safely retry without risking conflicting operations.
This approach ensures that clients can recover from transient failures while maintaining system consistency and avoiding duplicate state mutations.
Tracing a command through a three-node cluster reveals how Raft coordinates consensus.
A client sends a request to the leader, which appends it to its log and replicates it to followers.
Once a majority acknowledges the entry, the leader commits it and applies it to its state machine.
Followers apply the entry in order after replication.
If the leader fails, followers detect the missing heartbeats and trigger elections.
A new leader is elected, and replication resumes from the last committed entry.
This trace demonstrates how partial failures, log replication, and majority quorums work together to maintain consistency.
The process ensures that every command is processed exactly once, even during network delays or node crashes, providing a reliable foundation for distributed applications.
